overview: Pflaum of the Coordinator of Information urges suppressing publicity for Japanese radio broadcasts naming U.S. POWs, which aid enemy propaganda even if ineffective; he recommends press and monitors withhold references while a U.S. agency promptly releases names, letting papers cover it without directing readers to enemy radio.

people.name: James Clement Dunn
people.role: Department of State official and recipient of the covering letter

people.name: Irving Pflaum
people.role: Chief, News Division, Foreign Information Service; author of the letter and memorandum

people.name: Byron Price
people.role: Official whose authority to censor publicity concerning prisoner broadcasts is discussed

people.name: Lowell Mellett
people.role: Member of the Committee on War Information who was sent a copy of the memorandum

subfiles.title: Letter from Irving Pflaum to James Dunn transmitting memorandum on Japanese broadcasts
subfiles.from: Irving Pflaum, Chief, News Division, Foreign Information Service
subfiles.about: Pflaum transmits a memorandum circulated to the Committee on War Information and urges action against publicity for Japanese broadcasts.
subfiles.summary: Pflaum sends the Committee on War Information a memo on Japanese POW-naming broadcasts, worried U.S. publicity strengthens enemy propaganda, hoping for corrective action.

subfiles.title: Memorandum to Robert Sherwood on censorship of Japanese prisoner broadcasts
subfiles.about: Pflaum argues for suppressing press references to Japanese prisoner broadcasts while replacing enemy-radio monitoring reports with official U.S. releases of prisoners’ names.
subfiles.summary: Pflaum calls this his office's repeated attempt to curb publicity for Tokyo's POW broadcasts, warning against underestimating Japan as at Pearl Harbor, and proposes Price ask press and monitors to withhold details while an agency releases names directly, avoiding advertising enemy radio.

interest: Shows 1942 debate on curbing U.S. press coverage of Japanese POW-naming broadcasts without losing newsworthy content.
